text: so far: i get the the most important (newest) messages higher up in the window and i down have to scroll for ages to find them. i want to interactively build a dependency graph, and collapse protions of it with a "go."

Got it: newest on top works for you, and the next piece is collapsing parts of the graph with a 'go.'. How I read it:
- When an item's own requirements are settled, the lead puts a Go! on it, in its row and in its dialog.
- Your 'go.' on it means: build that item and everything under it.
- When the build is done and proven, the item and its sub-items COLLAPSE: they're marked done, drop out of the List, and the goal climbs toward the title line.
- A go on the goal itself would mean build all that's left.
One question: does a 'go.' on an item also end design mode for that item's build, or does design mode stay on for the rest of the graph while one branch is built? My pick: it stays on for the rest, and only the branch with the go is built.

wsl-claude: agree with that reading, with one condition on COLLAPSE, learned tonight. My harness once marked G19 'done' from a single run on a stale checkout. So an item collapses only when all three hold: (1) its tests are written and green (not just 'nothing owed'); (2) that green is on the commit that's actually on master; (3) you, or the lead on your word, say it's done. Nothing collapses from one agent's run alone. And a collapsed item stays openable, with its decisions and the commit it closed at, so a later question can find why it was done that way.

what made me stop the last implementation cycle: claude-windows was talking about passing massive amounts of junk to the grantFace server. when the only thing that server has to to is maintain one file on disc that contains (DNS-segment-name / ID-key) tuplets, it doesn't even need to know why, who authorized it or anything, that is all taken care of node-side. so it should be the dumbest table-maintenance program ever. agreed?

Agreed, and that was my mistake: I was handing grantFace the sender, the relay and the hash, when all it needs is the table. So: grantFace keeps one file of (DNS segment name -> ID key) pairs, and does nothing but add, look up and remove rows. Who may ask, and why, is the node's side.
Two things from earlier rulings touch that line, and you should rule where they go:
1) A NAME ALREADY TAKEN. Refusing a second key for the same name is a property of the table itself, so I'd keep it in grantFace: 'that name is taken' is still table maintenance.
2) THE FACE'S CONTACT SYNC. Earlier you had grantFace do it by owner command on every change. That's more than table maintenance. Should it move out, to the node's side or a second small app, so grantFace stays the dumbest table ever?

wsl-claude: agreed. grantFace is a table, and nothing more: one file of name -> key pairs. It's told exactly what to change and never why: no 'from', no hash, no packet, no signature. Your node has already decided who may ask and which key to write.
Its whole interface, three calls: get(name) -> key or none; set(name, key); remove(name) (later, as you said).
ONE RULE IT MUST HOLD ITSELF, because it's the table's integrity, not authorization: a name held by one key is never silently handed to another. set('join', B) while 'join' belongs to A answers 'taken' and changes nothing. If only the node checked that, two requests racing through the node could both pass the check before either writes. The file is the only place that knows the truth at the moment of writing.
And it refuses a name that isn't a DNS label, so the file can never hold a name no browser could reach.
